about.title: Systems of Linear Inequalities: Finding the Points That Obey Every Rule
audience: anyone relearning algebra at a gentle pace
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are two linked ideas: graphing the overlap, then reading real-life limits as constraints. Both fit in a half-hour if you pause at each question. If you need more time, stop after the four-step recipe and do the game-shop part in a second sitting.

Graphing Systems of Linear Inequalities (CK-12 Algebra I Concepts Honors, section 5.6)

say.text: Welcome back. Today's goal: graph two or more rules at the same time, then find the points that obey every rule. Take your time, and pause whenever you like.

show.text: Systems of Linear Inequalities

say.text: First, the name. A system of linear inequalities is two or more inequalities grouped together. It looks like a system of equations, but it uses inequality signs.

show.text: System of linear inequalities

say.text: Quick recap on ONE inequality. Its solutions fill one side of a boundary line. A strict sign, < or >, leaves the line itself out, so we draw that line dashed.

show.text: ≤ or ≥ : line is included (solid) | < or > : line is left out (dashed)

ask.q: For y < x + 1, are the points ON the boundary line part of the solution?
ask.right: No. A strict sign leaves the line out, so we draw it dashed.
wrong: Yes. Every boundary line is always part of the solution.
Only the point (0, 1) on the line counts.
It depends on what colour you shade with.
ask.why: The sign < means strictly less than. Points on the line make y equal to x + 1, so they don't satisfy it.

say.text: Now the key rule for a system. A point is a solution only if it makes EVERY inequality true. One true and one false is not enough.

show.text: True for ALL of them

say.text: Here is our system: y ≥ 2x − 1 and y < x + 1. Test the point (−1, −1). First: −1 ≥ 2(−1) − 1 is −1 ≥ −3. True. Second: −1 < −1 + 1 is −1 < 0. True too.

show.text:
y ≥ 2x − 1
y < x + 1
Test (−1, −1): −1 ≥ −3 true, and −1 < 0 true

say.text: Both true, so (−1, −1) is a solution. Now try (3, 0). First rule: 0 ≥ 2(3) − 1 is 0 ≥ 5. False. One false is enough, so (3, 0) is out.

show.text: Test (3, 0): 0 ≥ 5 is false, so not a solution

ask.q: Is (0, 0) a solution of y ≥ 2x − 1 and y < x + 1?
ask.right: Yes. 0 ≥ −1 is true, and 0 < 1 is true.
wrong: No. 0 < 1 is false.
No. (0, 0) sits on a boundary line, so it never counts.
Only the first inequality matters, so it depends on that one alone.
ask.why: Put x = 0 and y = 0 into each rule. Both come out true, and that is what a solution needs.

say.text: Testing one point at a time is slow. A graph shows ALL the solutions at once. Step 1: graph the first inequality. Draw y = 2x − 1 as a solid line, because of ≥.

show.text: A coordinate grid. A solid line crosses the y-axis at −1 and rises 2 up for every 1 right. The area above the line is shaded light blue.

say.text: How do we know which side to shade? Pick a test point. (0, 0) gives 0 ≥ −1, which is true, so we shade the side with (0, 0). That is above the line.

show.text: Test point (0, 0): true, so shade its side

say.text: Step 2: on the SAME grid, graph the second inequality. Draw y = x + 1 as a dashed line, because of <. Test (0, 0): 0 < 1 is true, so shade below this line.

show.text: Same grid. A dashed line crosses the y-axis at 1 and rises 1 up for every 1 right. The area below the dashed line is shaded light yellow.

say.text: Step 3: look for where the two shadings overlap. The double-shaded part is the solution. Here it is a wedge opening toward the left, and it holds (−1, −1).

show.text: The blue and yellow shadings overlap in a wedge. Its corner is at (2, 3) and it opens to the left. The point (−1, −1) is inside it, marked with a dot.

say.text: Look at the corner where the lines cross. Setting 2x − 1 = x + 1 gives x = 2 and y = 3. That crossing point is not a solution here, because the second line is dashed.

show.text: Crossing point (2, 3): not included

ask.q: The lines cross at (2, 3). Is (2, 3) a solution of the system?
ask.right: No. In y < x + 1 we get 3 < 3, which is false.
wrong: Yes. A crossing point always counts.
Yes, because 3 ≥ 2(2) − 1 is true, so one rule is enough.
No, because it is outside the graph.
ask.why: The point passes the first rule but fails the second, which is strict. It has to pass both.

say.text: Here is the whole recipe. Graph the first inequality. Graph the second on the same grid. The solution is where the shading overlaps. Then check with a test point.

show.text:
1. Graph the first inequality (line, then shade)
2. Graph the second on the same grid
3. The solution is where the shading overlaps
4. Check with a test point

say.text: The official standard says the same thing in grown-up words. The solution set is the intersection of the half-planes. Intersection just means the overlap.

show.text: Graph the solution set ... as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

say.text: Now real life. Real life puts limits on us, like money, time and space. Each limit is a constraint, and we write it as an inequality.

show.text: Constraint = a limit, written as an inequality

say.text: The points that obey all the constraints form the feasible region. 'Feasible' just means possible. Any point in that region is a workable choice.

show.text: Feasible region = all the possible choices

ask.q: What does it mean if a point is inside the feasible region?
ask.right: It obeys every constraint, so it is a possible choice.
wrong: It breaks at least one constraint.
It sits on exactly one boundary line and nowhere else.
It is always the best possible choice.
ask.why: The feasible region is where all the constraints overlap. Being inside it means passing every rule, not that the choice is the best one.

say.text: A made-up example. Sam has $20 in a game shop. Skins cost $4 each, and boosts cost $2 each. The shop allows at most 6 items per player.

show.text:
x = number of skins ($4 each)
y = number of boosts ($2 each)
Budget: $20
Shop limit: 6 items

say.text: Turn each limit into an inequality. First say it in words, then write the symbols. Money: 4x + 2y ≤ 20. Items: x + y ≤ 6. And you can't buy a negative amount, so x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

show.text:
Money: 4x + 2y ≤ 20
Items: x + y ≤ 6
No negatives: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0

ask.q: Which inequality says Sam's total spending is at most $20?
ask.why: Skins cost $4 each, so they add 4x. Boosts cost $2 each, so they add 2y. 'At most' means ≤.

say.text: To draw the money line 4x + 2y = 20, find where it hits the axes. If x = 0, then 2y = 20, so y = 10. If y = 0, then x = 5. The points are (0, 10) and (5, 0).

show.text: Money line: (0, 10) and (5, 0) | Item line x + y = 6: (0, 6) and (6, 0)

ask.q: On the money line 4x + 2y = 20, what is y when x = 0?
ask.why: With x = 0 the equation becomes 2y = 20. Dividing both sides by 2 gives y = 10.

say.text: Now shade. Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 20 is true and 0 ≤ 6 is true, so shade below both lines. The rules x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 keep us in the top-right part of the grid.

show.text: A grid in the top-right quarter only. Two solid lines slope down: one from (0, 10) to (5, 0) and one from (0, 6) to (6, 0). The area under both lines is shaded.

say.text: The overlap is a four-sided shape with corners at (0, 0), (5, 0), (4, 2) and (0, 6). The corner (4, 2) is where the two lines cross: 16 + 4 = 20, and 4 + 2 = 6.

show.text: A four-sided shaded shape with corners (0,0), (5,0), (4,2) and (0,6). The corner (4,2) is circled where the two slanted lines meet.

say.text: Now test some orders. (3, 3): money is 12 + 6 = 18, which is at most 20, and items are 6, which is at most 6. Feasible. (5, 1): money is 20 + 2 = 22, which is over 20. Not feasible.

show.text: (3, 3): 18 ≤ 20 and 6 ≤ 6, feasible | (5, 1): 22 > 20, not feasible

ask.q: Is buying 2 skins and 5 boosts, the point (2, 5), feasible?
ask.right: No. That is 7 items, and the limit is 6.
wrong: Yes. The cost is 18, which is under 20, so it is fine.
Yes, because both numbers are positive.
No, because it costs more than $20.
ask.why: The money rule passes, since 8 + 10 = 18. But 2 + 5 = 7 breaks the item limit, and one broken rule makes the order infeasible.

say.text: One real-life twist. You can't buy half a skin. So Sam's real choices are the whole-number points inside the region, like (3, 3) or (1, 4).

show.text: Real choices: whole-number points inside the region

ask.q: Which order can Sam actually make: (2.5, 1) or (2, 1)?
ask.right: (2, 1). The numbers are whole, and 8 + 2 = 10 is within budget.
wrong: (2.5, 1), because it is inside the region.
Both, because both are inside the region.
Neither, because both cost too much.
ask.why: Items come in whole numbers. (2, 1) costs $10 and is 3 items, so it passes every rule.

say.text: Sometimes the limits fight each other. Say Sam insists on spending at least $30 with only $20. Then 4x + 2y ≥ 30 and 4x + 2y ≤ 20 are parallel lines with no overlap, so there is no feasible region.

show.text: Two parallel slanted lines. The shading above the upper one and the shading below the lower one point away from each other and never overlap.

ask.q: Do parallel boundary lines always mean a system has no solution?
ask.right: No. Some parallel systems overlap in a strip between the lines, and some don't overlap at all.
wrong: Yes, parallel lines always mean no solution.
Yes, but only when both lines are dashed.
No, they always give exactly one solution point.
ask.why: It depends on which way each one is shaded. For example, 4x + 2y ≥ 10 and 4x + 2y ≤ 20 overlap in the strip between the lines.

say.text: A peek ahead. The corners of a feasible region matter. A method called linear programming tests the corner points to find a best answer, like the most profit or the lowest cost.

show.text: Corners of the region: where the best answers hide

say.text: Recap. A system means all rules at once. Graph each one, find the overlap, and test a point. In real problems the overlap is the feasible region. Last check, and well done for sticking with it.

show.text:
System = all rules true at once
Graph each inequality on one grid
Solution = the overlap
Real problems: constraints give a feasible region

ask.q: Which point is a solution of y ≥ 2x − 1 and y < x + 1?
ask.why: (−2, −3): −3 ≥ −5 is true and −3 < −1 is true. (3, 0) fails the first rule, (2, 3) fails the second, and (0, 2) fails the second because 2 < 1 is false.

other_side.claim: The solution of a system is the double-shaded (darkest) region of the graph.
other_side.other_view: OpenStax describes the solution as the region shaded twice, so it looks darker. CK-12 notes that it is common to erase the shading that isn't part of the solution, so the answer is easy to see. Both ways are fine. Erasing can help when there are three or more inequalities and the picture gets crowded.
